In [[mathematics]], '''even and odd ordinals''' extend the concept of [[parity (mathematics)|parity]] from the [[natural number]]s to the [[ordinal number]]s. They are useful in some [[transfinite induction]] [[Mathematical proof|proofs]].

The literature contains a few equivalent definitions of the parity of an ordinal α:

*Zero and each [[limit ordinal]] are even. The [[successor ordinal|successor]] of an even ordinal is odd, and vice versa.<ref>{{cite book |title=Real Analysis |author1=Bruckner, Andrew M. |author2=Judith B. Bruckner |author3=Brian S. Thomson |name-list-style=amp |year=1997 |isbn=0-13-458886-X |pages=[https://archive.org/details/realanalysis00bruc/page/37 37] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/realanalysis00bruc/page/37 }}</ref><ref name="Salzmann">{{cite book |author=Salzmann, H., T. Grundhöfer, H. Hähl, and R. Löwen |title=The Classical Fields: Structural Features of the Real and Rational Numbers |pages=[https://archive.org/details/classicalfieldss0000unse/page/168 168] |year=2007 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-86516-6 |url=https://archive.org/details/classicalfieldss0000unse/page/168 }}</ref>
*Let α = λ + ''n'', where λ is a limit ordinal and ''n'' is a natural number. The parity of α is the parity of ''n''.<ref>{{cite book |title=Fundamentals of Real Analysis |first=James |last=Foran |year=1991 |publisher=CRC Press |pages=[https://archive.org/details/fundamentalsofre0000fora/page/110 110] |isbn=0-8247-8453-7 |url=https://archive.org/details/fundamentalsofre0000fora/page/110 }}</ref>
*Let ''n'' be the finite term of the [[Cantor normal form]] of α. The parity of α is the parity of ''n''.<ref>{{cite book |title=Ordered Sets |url=https://archive.org/details/orderedsets00harz_919 |url-access=limited |first=Egbert |last=Harzheim |pages=[https://archive.org/details/orderedsets00harz_919/page/n301 296] |year=2005 |publisher=Springer |isbn=0-387-24219-8}}</ref>
*Let α = ωβ + ''n'', where ''n'' is a natural number. The parity of α is the parity of ''n''.<ref name="Kamke">{{cite book |title=Theory of Sets |first=Erich |last=Kamke |pages=96 |year=1950 |publisher=Courier Dover |isbn=0-486-60141-2}}</ref>
*If α = 2β, then α is even. Otherwise α = 2β + 1 and α is odd.<ref name="Kamke" /><ref>{{cite book |title=Set Theory |first=Felix |last=Hausdorff |authorlink=Felix Hausdorff |pages=99 |year=1978 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=0-8284-0119-5}}</ref>

Unlike the case of even [[integer]]s, one cannot go on to characterize even ordinals as ordinal numbers of the form {{nowrap|1=β2 = β + β.}} [[Ordinal multiplication]] is not commutative, so in general {{nowrap|2β ≠ β2.}} In fact, the even ordinal {{nowrap|ω + 4}} cannot be expressed as β + β, and the ordinal number
:(ω + 3)2 = (ω + 3) + (ω + 3) = ω + (3 + ω) + 3 = ω + ω + 3 = ω2 + 3
is not even.

A simple application of ordinal parity is the [[idempotence]] law for [[cardinal addition]] (given the [[well-ordering theorem]]). Given an infinite cardinal κ, or generally any limit ordinal κ, κ is order-isomorphic to both its subset of even ordinals and its subset of odd ordinals. Hence one has the cardinal sum {{nowrap|1=κ + κ = κ.}}<ref name="Salzmann" /><ref>{{cite book |title=Introduction to Modern Set Theory |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontomo0000roit |url-access=registration |first=Judith |last=Roitman |pages=[https://archive.org/details/introductiontomo0000roit/page/88 88] |year=1990 |publisher=Wiley-IEEE |isbn=0-471-63519-7}}</ref>
